segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this I looked, and there was a door standing open in heaven, and the first voice that I had heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: at once I was in the Spirit; and there was a throne standing in heaven, and on the throne someone was seated.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one seated was like jasper stone and carnelian in appearance, and around the throne was a rainbow like emerald in appearance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Around the throne were twenty-four thrones, and on the thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From the throne came flashes of lightning and rumblings and peals of thunder. Seven torches of fire were burning before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and before the throne was something like a sea of glass, like crystal. In the middle of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes in front and behind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The first living creature was like a lion, the second living creature like an ox, the third living creature had a face like that of a human, and the fourth living creature was like an eagle in flight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The four living creatures, each one of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never rest, saying:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is coming.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And whenever the living creatures give glory and honour and thanks to the one seated on the throne, who lives forever and ever,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the twenty-four elders fall down before the one seated on the throne and worship the one who lives forever and ever, and they throw their crowns before the throne, saying:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive the glory and the honour and the power, for you created all things, and because of your will they existed and were created.”

notes.traditional: what must take place after this
notes.note: The closing words of the verse can be attached either to the speech ('what must take place after this') or to the next sentence ('After this, at once I was in the Spirit'). Most English translations take the first option, which echoes Daniel 2 in the Greek Old Testament. This translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition used, which begins a new sentence here.

notes.phrase: the first voice that I had heard
notes.note: This points back to the trumpet-like voice of 1:10, where John turns and sees the risen Jesus. On that basis the words are attributed to Jesus here, as most interpreters hold. Some think instead that the voice belongs to an angel who introduces the visions.

The Greek has no article and could also mean 'in spirit', that is, in a visionary state as opposed to bodily. Most translations take it as a reference to God's Spirit as the source of the prophetic vision, as at 1:10. The two readings are not far apart in practice.

The word normally means a torch, a blazing brand, not the small oil lamp of a household, for which Greek has a different word. Older English versions and some modern ones have 'lamps'. Several recent translations also use 'torches'.

Many interpreters take this as a symbolic way of speaking of the one Spirit of God in its fullness, seven being the number of completeness, and some translations capitalise accordingly. Others understand seven chief angels who stand before God, an idea known in Jewish writings of the period. The translation leaves 'spirits' in lower case and does not decide the question.

notes.phrase: In the middle of the throne and around the throne
notes.note: The Greek is hard to picture. It may mean that the creatures stand in the immediate vicinity of the throne, one on each side of it, or that they are in some way part of the throne itself, as the cherubim are in Old Testament throne imagery. The translation keeps the literal wording.

The scene draws on two Old Testament visions: the four living creatures with the faces of a human, lion, ox and eagle in Ezekiel 1, and the six-winged seraphim who cry 'Holy, holy, holy' in Isaiah 6. The word used here is a different one from the 'beast' of later chapters, although the King James Version translated both as 'beast'.

The word can mean a calf, but in the Greek Old Testament it is used widely for bulls and oxen, including for the ox-faced creature of Ezekiel 1:10, which this verse echoes. English versions are divided between 'calf' and 'ox'.

The Greek is a present participle, 'the coming one', not a future form of 'to be'. Where one might expect 'who will be', the title says that God is on his way. 'Who is to come' is the usual rendering and is not wrong, but 'who is coming' keeps the sense of approach.

The verbs in verses 9 and 10 are future in Greek ('whenever they will give ... the elders will fall'). Most translators take this as describing repeated, customary action, possibly under Semitic influence, and use the present tense, as here. A minority take it as a real future, pointing forward to the acts of worship narrated later in the book.

notes.phrase: throw their crowns before the throne
notes.note: The word covers both a wreath given as a prize or honour and a royal crown; a different word is used later in the book for the diadem of a ruler. Laying one's crown before another was a recognised gesture of submission by subject rulers to an overlord. The elders acknowledge that their honour is derived from the one on the throne.

The Roman writer Suetonius reports that the emperor Domitian was addressed as 'our lord and god'. Many scholars hear a deliberate counter-claim in this acclamation, since Revelation is commonly dated to his reign. The link is plausible but not certain, and the pairing 'Lord' and 'God' is also thoroughly biblical.

The Greek construction expresses the reason or ground for something, not the means: creation exists because God willed it. Most modern versions have 'by your will'; the King James Version has 'for thy pleasure'. The difference is small, but 'because of' is the more exact rendering.

candidates.reason: Must be kept consistently distinct from θηρίον ('beast') across Revelation, which the KJV blurred by using 'beast' for both.
Translators vary between 'crown' and 'wreath', and readers need it distinguished consistently from διάδημα across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation.
Recurs throughout the Gospels and Revelation, where the choice between 'worship', 'bow down' and 'pay homage' carries theological weight and should not vary arbitrarily.
A Septuagint title, often standing for 'of hosts', that recurs nine times in Revelation and in 2 Corinthians 6:18 and should be rendered uniformly.
